title: Senolytic Treatment Attenuates Global Ischemic Brain Injury and Enhances Cognitive Recovery by Targeting Mitochondria

sections.abstract:
The benefits of senolytic therapy have been known in a series of age-related diseases, whereas its potential roles in global cerebral ischemic (GCI) brain injury remain unexplored. In current study, we aim to investigate the effects of combined senolytics Dasatinib plus Quercetin (D&Q) treatment in GCI and the underlying mechanisms in a mouse model. We firstly report that 12-week post-GCI D&Q treatment effectively eliminated cellular senescence of astrocytes and microglia in the hippocampus of mice brain, followed by decreased release of the potent inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP). Further mechanistic analysis suggested that D&Q administration can effectively regulate mitochondrial function as a critical downstream target. D&Q treatment inhibited GCI-induced mitochondrial fragmentation and maintained mitochondrial integrity. Subsequently, D&Q treatment improved the mitochondrial metabolic function by enhancing mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity and ATP production. Moreover, D&Q treatment reversed the decline of mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme SOD2 and reduced the ROS accumulation and suppressed oxidative damage to cellular protein structure. Further investigation indicated D&Q treatment protected the hippocampal neurons after GCI by mitigating the dendritic injury and neuronal apoptotic signaling. Extensive behavioral tests assessed the functional outcomes and showed that D&Q treatment effectively preserved hippocampus-dependent spatial reference memory and recognition memory, and mitigated GCI-induced anxiety and depression levels. Taken together, our study provides leading evidence for the neuroprotective roles of the senolytics D&Q in GCI model and identifies regulation of mitochondrial functions could be the key underlying mechanism. These findings offer novel insights into the potential clinical applications of senolytic agents in therapy.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10571-025-01580-y.

Keywords: Senolytics, Senescence, Ischemic brain injury, Neuroprotection, Inflammation, Mitochondria
sections.introduction:
Global cerebral ischemia (GCI) triggered by clinical conditions such as cardiac arrest and asphyxia, is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, inflicting 4–5 million people each year (Neumann et al. 2013 ; Chugh et al. 2008 ; Goldberger et al. 2008 ). GCI results in sharp reduction of cerebral blood flow along with low oxygen and glucose supply to the brain. Such transient GCI and following reperfusion lead to a series of pathological cascades, including mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic abnormality, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation and eventually delayed neuronal damage in the brain especially in the hippocampus (Vatandoust et al. 2023 ; Estuani et al. 2023 ; Nakajima et al. 2022 ; Richmond 1997 ; Choi 1985 ). Neuroinflammation, in particular plays a critical role in the initiation of GCI-induced brain injury.

Neuroinflammation occurs immediately after cerebral ischemia–reperfusion and could last up to years in the chronic stage (Pluta et al. 2021 ). While acute neuroinflammation exerts beneficial effects, sustained neuroinflammation destructs the integrity of blood–brain barrier allowing excessive infiltration of peripheral immune cells, polarizes glia cells in the brain to pro-inflammatory phenotypes and exacerbates the secondary damage to neurons (Candelario-Jalil et al. 2022 ; DiSabato et al. 2016 ; Wang et al. 2022 ). Curbing the initiation of neuroinflammation and its downstream pathological signaling could thus be a key target in GCI therapy. Despite abundant efforts in past decades, the potential mechanisms of inflammation occurring after ischemic brain injury are still elusive. Further investigating the mechanisms underlying chronic inflammation after GCI and seeking new therapeutic strategies are thus urgently needed.

Emerging evidences suggest senescent cells accumulate in the brain following brain injury, aging and a variety of neurodegenerative diseases (Russo and Riessland 2022 ; Zhang et al. 2019 ; Baker et al. 2011 ). Cellular senescence, a cellular state characterized by irreversible cell proliferation arrest and resistance to dying is driven by persistent DNA damage which induces high level of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (CDKIs), like p16 (Ohtani et al. 2001 ). Featured by prolonged p16 and/or p21 activity and robust expression of senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal), cellular senescence has been demonstrated as a potent stimulus for inflammaging, chronic inflammation and neurodegeneration (Di Micco et al. 2021 ). Senescent cells can exacerbate the inflammatory environment and following neuronal damage by the release of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), including proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, proteases, growth factors and secreted proteins (Ohtani 2022 ; Acosta et al. 2013 ; Kuilman et al. 2008 ). Previous studies reported significantly elevated SASP-associated mediators after traumatic brain injury (TBI), including cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF, and chemokines CXCL10, CCL2 and CCL5 (Vaibhav et al. 2020 ; Woodcock and Morganti-Kossmann 2013 ). Such proinflammatory factors can simultaneously facilitate peripheral immune cell recruitment to the brain and further perpetuate neuroinflammatory damage (Hernandez-Segura et al. 2018 ; Jiang et al. 2017 ).

Many cell types in the brain especially glial cells like astrocytes and microglia, have been observed with senescent phenotypes in neural disorders. Senescent glial cells, identified by increased p16 INK4a expression are associated with accumulated neurotoxic beta-amyloid oligomers and contribute to Alzheimer’s disease pathology. (Stein et al. 2014 ). In addition, early microglial proliferation promotes replicative senescence and correlate with disease-associated microglia (DAM) and senescent microglial profiles in post-mortem AD cases (Hu et al. 2021 ). Interestingly, genetic elimination of p16 INK4A -positive senescent astrocytes and microglia prevented tau-dependent pathology and cognitive decline in a MAPT P301S PS19 mouse model (Bussian et al. 2018 ). Extensive studies across different disease models have demonstrated that the senolytics Dasatinib and Quercetin, FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors possess profound effects on clearing senescent cells by triggering apoptotic signaling pathways (Richardson and Richardson 2024 ; Musi et al. 2018 ; Yu et al. 2016 ; Yang et al. 2014 ). Despite the widely reported benefits, the effects of combined Dasatinib plus Quercetin (D&Q) treatment in GCI brain injury remain unclear. The current study was designed to explore the roles of D&Q post-treatment in a GCI mice model. Our study could provide new therapeutic options for future clinic trials.
sections.methods:
C57BL/6J male mice at 3-month age were used in current study. All animals were kept in a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle at 22 ± 2 °C with free access to water and food before use. 3–5 mice were housed per cage. Mice were assigned into three groups ( N = 8): Sham, GCI and GCI plus D&Q treatment. GCI model was performed as previously described (Zhu et al. 2017 ). Briefly, mice were deeply anesthetized with phenobarbital and analgesic was administered at the time of anesthesia. GCI was induced with both common carotid arteries isolated and transiently occluded for 20 min. Mice were kept on a heating pad with the temperature maintained at 36.5–37.5 °C. During the procedure, blood flow through arteries was constantly monitored with a non-invasive laser speckle contrast imaging and rectal temperature was monitored with rectal thermal probe. Reduction of blood flow over 90% were considered successful and used as further studies. The surgical wound was sutured, and mice were returned to their home cage for recovery. Sham mice were subjected to the same procedure, only without common carotid arteries occlusion. All experimental procedures and protocols were reviewed and approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Kangda College of Nanjing Medical University (No. 303201121111) and were performed in accordance with the Guidelines for the Chinese Experimental Animal Administration Legislation. All the experimental participants were randomly assigned and double-blind study was used in current study. It’s noted that sample size adopted here was based on previous studies, not determined by a priori sample size calculation, which we consider as a study limitation.

D&Q treatment was performed as previously reported (Saccon et al. 2021 ). Dasatinib (Sigma, CDS023389-25MG, 5 mg/kg) plus quercetin (Sigma, Q4951-10G, 50 mg/kg) were dissolved in a solution comprising 10% ethanol, 30% polyethylene glycol 400 and 60% Phosal 50 PG. These dosages of Dasatinib and Quercetin were chosen based on safety and general senolytic effects in mice from previous studies (Wang et al. 2023 ; Saccon et al. 2021 ). D&Q treatment was given at 1 day after GCI injury with oral gavage for 3 consecutive days a week for 12 weeks. GCI control mice were given the same volume of dissolving solution as the treatment group.

SASP levels in mice hippocampus were measured with multiplex assays (Bio-Techne, Cat# LXSAMSM). Hippocampal homogenates were made as previously described with minor revisions (Zhang et al. 2020 ). Briefly, brain tissue was quickly collected following transcardic perfusion with cold saline. Hippocampus was separated and homogenized with a motor-driven Teflon homogenizer in 400 μl ice-cold homogenization buffer, which contained protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL). The homogenates were then mixed for 20 min on a rotator at 4 °C and centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 min to get total protein fractions in the supernatant. The protein concentration was determined with Protein Assay Dye Reagent Concentrate (BioRad). The obtained protein lysates were stored at − 80 °C until use. Levels of key SASP factors, including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, CCL2, CXCL1 and CXCL5 were measured with Mouse Luminex® Discovery Assay from Bio-Techne and analyzed as a unit of pg/mg protein.

Mice brain sections were prepared as previously described (Tu et al. 2021 ). Briefly, mice were transcardially perfused with ice-cold saline, followed by subsequent 4% paraformaldehyde under deep anesthesia. Brain tissues were quickly removed after decapitation, and then subjected to fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde at 4 °C for 48 h. Mice brains were subsequently transferred to 30% sucrose at 4 °C until sink. The tissues were then embedded in tissue embedding medium (Fisher HealthCare, 4585), and cut into 20 μm thickness of frozen sections with Leica microtome. Immunofluorescent staining was performed with the following primary antibodies: GFAP (Invitrogen, Cat# PA5-16,291, RRID: AB_10980769); IBA1 (proteintech, Cat# 10,904-1-AP, RRID: AB_2224377); p16INK4a (Invitrogen, Cat# MA5-17,142, RRID: AB_2538613); Tom20 (Santa Cruz, Cat# sc-17764, RRID: AB_628381); NeuN (proteintech, Cat# 66836-1-Ig, RRID: AB_2882179); Cleaved-Caspase 3 (Invitrogen, Cat# PA5-114687, RRID: AB_2899323); MAP2 (Invitrogen, Cat# PA5-17646, RRID: AB_11006358). Fluorescent images were captured on an LSM510 Meta confocal laser microscope (Carl Zeiss), and analyzed with LSM510 Meta imaging software. Intensity value was further measured with ImageJ software. At least 4–5 representative sections per animal were used for immunostaining, and the typical image was selected for presentation. It’s noted that since the specificities of antibodies used above were demonstrated by the vendors, no further validation was performed in current study.

Hippocampal protein homogenate was prepared as previously described (Park et al. 2019 ). Briefly, hippocampus was quickly collected under deep anesthesia after transcardial perfusion with ice-cold 0.9% saline. Hippocampus was then homogenized with a motor-driven Teflon homogenizer in 400 μl ice-cold homogenization buffer that contained protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The homogenates were then vigorously mixed for 20 min on a rotator at 4 °C and centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 20 min to get total protein fractions in the supernatant. Protein concentration was measured with Protein Assay Dye Reagent Concentrate (BioRad). Western blot was performed as previously described (Park et al. 2019 ). The primary antibodies used in current study include SOD2 (Cell Signaling, Cat# 13,141, RRID: AB_2636921, 1:1000) and GAPDH (Invitrogen, Cat# PA1-987, RRID: AB_2107311, 1:5000). Gels were imaged on a CCD digital imaging system and band intensities were analyzed with ImageJ software. SOD2 levels of all groups were normalized to GAPDH and diagramed as fold changes to Sham. Full plot was shown in the supplement.

Dihydroethidium (DHE) staining was carried out to measure the total ROS levels (Wang and Zou 2018 ). Briefly, brain sections were incubated with 10 μM DHE (AnaSpec) in darkness for 10 min at room temperature. After 3 × 10 min washes with PBS, sections were mounted on slide for visualization under confocal microscope. The fluorescence intensity was measured at 485 nm excitation/590 nm emission. Mean intensity of DHE florescence in hippocampus CA1 region was quantitively analyzed with ImageJ software.

Protein carbonyls in the hippocampus were measured with a high-sensitivity OxiSelect™ ELISA kit (CELL BIOLAB, CAT# STA-310) to analyze the oxidative stress levels. Based on vendor’s instruction, 100 µL of 10 μg/mL protein sample was incubated in the 96-well Protein Binding Plate at 4 °C overnight. After 3 times washes with 250 µL 1X PBS, plate was incubated with 100 µL of the DNPH Working Solution for 45 min at room temperature in the dark, followed by wash with 250 µL of 1X PBS/Ethanol (1:1, v/v) and 1X PBS. 200 µL of Blocking Solution was added afterwards for 2-h incubation at room temperature followed by 3 times 1X PBS wash. 100 µL of the diluted anti-DNP antibody was then added for 1-h incubation and 3 times 1X PBS wash was performed. After another incubation with 100 µL of HRP conjugated secondary antibody for 1-h, 5 times wash with 1X PBS and 100 μL of Substrate Solution incubation, the reaction was stopped by adding 100 µL of Stop Solution. The absorbance was immediately read on a plate reader on 450 nm. Protein carbonyl level was calculated with the established standard curve.

Cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity in mitochondria was measured with an CCO activity ELISA kit (ab109911, Abcam Inc) according to vendor’s instructions. Briefly, CCO enzyme was immunocaptured within the 96-well microplate which was pre-coated with antibody. The CCO activity was determined colorimetrical by following the oxidation of reduced cytochrome c as an absorbance decrease at 550 nm. ATP concentration was determined using a kit of ENLITEN rLuciferase/Luciferin reagent (FF2021, Promega, Madison, WI, USA) as previously described (Vultaggio-Poma et al. 2022 ). Briefly, 30 μg of sample proteins from total protein fractions were suspended in 100 μL of reconstituted rL/L reagent buffer containing luciferase, D-luciferin, Tris–acetate buffer (pH 7.75), EDTA, magnesium acetate, bovine serum albumin and dithiothreitol. Light emission at 10-s intervals from the reaction was measured in a standard microplate luminometer (PE Applied Biosystems). Relative light units from “background blank” containing rL/L reagent and the homogenization buffer used to prepare the samples were subtracted from the sample light output in the assay. ATP levels were determined using an ATP standard curve. Values of CCO activity and ATP levels were shown as percentage changes versus Sham group for graphical depiction.

Barnes Maze Test was performed at 85 days after GCI to test the hippocampus-dependent spatial reference memory (Zhang et al. 2020 ). A circular platform with 18 equally spaced holes around the perimeter was used for the maze platform. A camera connected to ANY-Maze tracking software was installed above the testing platform. Briefly, the test was divided into two stages: training stage (day 1 to day 3) and probe stage (day 4). During the training stage, mice were tested once a day with a duration of no more than 180 s. One hole was set as the target hole with a hidden escape chamber put beneath. At the beginning of each test, mice were located in the center of the platform, and bright light and aversive noise were used to impel animals to search for the hidden chamber. Test stopped when mice enter the target box. Escape latency to find the hidden chamber and escape velocity were recorded. During the probe stage, the hidden chamber was removed and mice were allowed to explore for 90 s. Exploring time in the target zone and numbers of exploration errors were recorded. Exploration error is defined as exploring any hole that does not have a hidden chamber beneath it. All the exploration activities were recorded and analyzed in ANY-Maze.

Novel object recognition test is widely used to evaluate the hippocampus-dependent recognition memory in rodents. As previously described (Wang et al. 2021 ), mice were tested in a black open arena with a dimension of 40 × 40 × 30 cm. A camera connected to ANY-Maze tracking software was installed above the box. The test was divided into two stages: sampling and choice stages. One day before test, mice were located in the open arena for a 5-min free exploration and habituation. On sampling stage, two same objects were placed in the open box with equal distance to the walls, and mice were placed into the arena for 5-min exploration. Choice stage was performed 24 h later. On choice stage, one of the objects was replaced with a novel object of similar size, but different shape. Mice were allowed for 5-min exploration. The exploration activity and total exploration time on each object were tracked by ANY-Maze software. The discrimination index was defined as the percentage of time exploring on the novel object in total exploration time.

Open field test was carried out to assess the anxiety level and locomotor function (Salazar et al. 2012 ). Briefly, mice were placed in an open arena (40 × 40 × 30 cm) for 5-min exploration. A camera connected to ANY-Maze tracking software was installed above the box. Total travel distance and time spent in central zone (20 × 20 cm) were recorded.

Tail suspension test was adopted here to assess the depression level. As previously described (Ito et al. 2012 ), mice were suspended by its tail from a hanger attached to a precision linear load cell. During the 6-min hanging time, their behaviors were recorded using videography. Mice that climbed their tail or fell off the hanger were excluded from analysis. Since all mice were uniformly active for the first minute, immobility time during the last 5 min were analyzed as a parameter of depression level.

All data in current study were expressed as mean ± SD. Shapiro–Wilk Test and Levene's test were used for normality and variance homogeneity test, respectively, P > 0.05 was assumed normality and homogeneity of variance (data were shown in the supplement). A Student’s T test was conducted when only comparing two groups. When comparing multiple groups difference, one-way ANOVA was performed followed by Tukey’s all pairwise comparisons. All the data were analyzed with GraphPad Prism 8 software. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results:
Glial activation-induced neuroinflammation after brain injury drives cellular senescence, which exacerbates inflammatory responses, aberrant metabolic changes, mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal damage (Amgalan et al. 2022 ; Schwab et al. 2021 ; Tominaga et al. 2019 ). To determine glial senescence levels in hippocampus and if D&Q treatment could attenuate this senescence development at 12 weeks after GCI, we performed immunofluorescent co-staining of glial markers with the typical senescence marker p16 INK4a . Double staining of GFAP, a classic marker of astrocyte with p16 INK4a (Fig. 1 A) showed GCI injury triggered robust astrocyte activation as evidenced by significantly elevated GFAP intensity (Fig. 1 B, a, p = 0.008). Interestingly, D&Q treatment reduced the GFAP intensity, suggesting an inhibitory effect on astrocyte activation (Fig. 1 B, a, p = 0.012). Further quantification of P16-positive astrocytes showed GCI-induced strong astrocytic senescence ( p = 0.007) which was attenuated by D&Q treatment as evidenced by decreased numbers of P16-positive astrocyte (Fig. 1 B, b, p < 0.001).

D&Q treatment attenuated glial senescence in mice hippocampus. A GFAP and p16 INK4a IF co-staining in hippocampal CA1 region was performed to examine astrocytic senescence among Sham, GCI and GCI + D&Q treatment groups. B GFAP relative fluorescence intensity compared to Sham ( a ) and Numbers of P16 + astrocytes ( b ) were quantitatively analyzed. Scale bar = 20 μm. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI. C IBA1 and p16 INK4a IF co-staining was performed to examine the senescence of hippocampal microglia in Sham, GCI and GCI + D&Q treatment groups. D IBA1 relative fluorescence intensity compared to Sham ( a ) and Numbers of P16 + microglia ( b ) were quantitatively analyzed. Scale bar = 20 μm. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI

To further examine the effects of D&Q treatment on microglial senescence, double staining of IBA1 and p16 INK4a was performed (Fig. 1 C). Quantitative analysis of IBA1 intensity indicated D&Q treatment was able to mitigate IBA1 expression, suggesting a reduced microglial activation after GCI (Fig. 1 D, a, p = 0.006). In addition, quantification of P16-positive microglia suggested a robustly decreased number after D&Q therapy, indicative of strong suppression on microglial senescence (Fig. 1 D, b, p < 0.001). These results demonstrate senolytic D&Q treatment can effectively attenuate glial senescence in mice hippocampus after GCI.

Senescent cells contribute to neural pathology by secreting potent pro-inflammatory SASP which includes a variety of cytokine and chemokine factors (Chinta et al. 2015 ). Next, we examined the expression of classic SASP factors in the hippocampus at 12 weeks after GCI, including cytokines IL-1 β, IL-6, TNF and chemokines CCL2, CXCL1 and CXCL5. Multiplex assays for hippocampal protein homogenate suggested that GCI-induced robust elevation in all these cytokines (IL1 β, IL-6, TNF) as compared to Sham, whereas D&Q treatment strongly suppressed these cytokines production (Fig. 2 A, p < 0.001 for IL-1β; p = 0.003 for IL-6; p < 0.001 for TNF). Similarly, we found D&Q treatment effectively decreased the hyperactivated chemokines CCL2, CXCL1 and CXCL5 after GCI (Fig. 2 B, p < 0.001 for CCL2; p = 0.002 for CXCL1; p = 0.041). These results demonstrated that D&Q treatment can profoundly curb senescence-associated pathology by suppressing these pro-inflammatory SASP factors after GCI brain injury.

Senescence-associated secretory phenotype was decreased after D&Q treatment. A Levels of classic SASP inflammatory cytokines in mice hippocampus, including IL1 β, IL-6 and TNF were measured with multiplex assays. B Classic SASP chemokines in hippocampus, including CCL2, CXCL1 and CXCL5 were measured with multiplex assays. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI

Mitochondria are vulnerable to inflammatory insult, and mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the major consequences of cellular senescence which is typically characterized by the morphological fragmentation (Miwa et al. 2022 ; Chapman et al. 2019 ). Next, we performed immunostaining of TOM20, a marker of mitochondria to assess the mitochondrial morphological changes in the hippocampus at 12 weeks following GCI insult (Fig. 3 A). By quantitative analysis we identified a drastic increase in total mitochondrial particle numbers (Fig. 3 B, a, p = 0.008) and mitochondrial fragmentation value after GCI (Fig. 3 B, b, p = 0.008). D&Q treatment, by contrast significantly reduced these mitochondrial particle numbers ( p = 0.01) and mitochondrial fragmentation value ( p = 0.016) as compared to GCI control (Fig. 3 B). There findings suggested that D&Q treatment can effectively preserve mitochondrial structural integrity after GCI injury by inhibiting mitochondrial fragmentation. We next evaluated mitochondrial metabolic function by measuring the activity of CCO IV, a key enzyme for mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and the final ATP production. ELISA assay with mitochondrial protein fractions showed decreased CCO activity (Fig. 3 C, p < 0.001) and ATP content (Fig. 3 D, p < 0.001) after GCI, suggesting impaired mitochondrial function and metabolic decline. Whereas D&Q treatment rescued the mitochondrial metabolic function by potentiating CCO activity ( p = 0.006) and subsequent ATP generation ( p < 0.001). These findings indicate that mitochondrial fragmentation and the subsequent energy failure are key pathological events following senescence-associated inflammatory insult, while maintaining mitochondrial metabolic function is a critical target of senolytics downstream actions.

D&Q treatment attenuated GCI-induced mitochondrial fragmentation and metabolic failure. A Mitochondrial morphology in hippocampus was visualized with TOM20 staining and further processed as Dot Plot in ImageJ. B Numbers of total mitochondrial particles were quantified ( a ) and mitochondrial fragmentation ( b ) were further analyzed. C and D Measurement of CCO activity ( C ) and ATP levels ( D ) using mitochondrial fractions and total protein fractions, respectively, to evaluate metabolic function. Scale bar = 5 μm. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI

Mitochondria contain efficient antioxidant enzymes to clear ROS which is generated as a byproduct during oxidative phosphorylation, and repair the oxidative damage to cellular molecules. We next examined the expression of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2), a major antioxidant enzyme to handle the ROS production in mitochondrial matrix. Western blot analysis suggested that the mitochondrial SOD2 was significantly decreased after GCI as compared to Sham (Fig. 4 A, p < 0.001). By contrast, D&Q treatment effectively reversed the declined SOD2 expression in GCI mice ( p = 0.022), suggesting improved mitochondrial antioxidant ability. DHE is generally linked to intracellular ROS level by forming a charged fluorescent species, ethidium within the cells. Therefore, DHE staining is widely used to monitor ROS generation. By performing DHE staining we showed that GCI mice exhibited robustly increased DHE intensity compared to Sham ( p = 0.008), which was suppressed by D&Q treatment (Fig. 4 B, p = 0.001). These results indicated a decreased ROS production after D&Q post-treatment in GCI mice following improved mitochondrial antioxidant ability.

D&Q treatment enhanced the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme, suppressed ROS accumulation and protein oxidation. A Western blot analysis of mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme SOD2 and the control protein GAPDH. Representative bands were shown above. B DHE, a fluorescence-derivative linked to ROS was stained to probe the ROS levels in hippocampus. C Protein carbonyl levels were analyzed with high-sensitivity ELISA kit to examine the protein oxidation. Scale bar = 20 μm. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI

We next detected a type of protein oxidation, protein carbonyl to confirm the oxidative damage to cellular protein structures. Using a high-sensitive protein carbonyl ELISA kit, our results suggested the surged total protein carbonyl level in hippocampus of GCI mice was significantly suppressed by D&Q treatment (Fig. 4 C, p = 0.007). This finding is consistent with our above results, demonstrating an inhibited oxidative damage to cellular structures after improved mitochondrial function.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and associated metabolic abnormality develop into eventual neuronal damage. Next, we examined the neuronal apoptotic signaling and dendritic morphological change in the hippocampus at 12 weeks after GCI brain injury. As shown in Fig. 5 A, double staining of NeuN, a neuronal marker and cleaved caspase 3 which is indicative of cellular apoptotic pathway, suggested there was a strong activation of apoptotic signaling after GCI as evidenced by hyperactivation of cl-caspase 3. In contrast, D&Q treatment robustly suppressed the cl-caspase 3 expression to a level similar to Sham group, which was validated by the quantitative analysis of cl-caspase 3-positive neurons ( p = 0.021) and relative cl-caspase 3 intensity ( p < 0.001) in Fig. 5 B. To evaluate the neuronal dendritic deficits, we next performed MAP2 staining (Fig. 5 C). Our results showed that mice subjected to GCI insult had significantly decreased total MAP2 fluorescence intensity ( p < 0.001) and elevated MAP2 dispersion value ( p = 0.008) in hippocampal CA1 region as compared to Sham (Fig. 5 D). D&Q treatment, by contrast significantly reversed these abnormal changes (Fig. 5 D, p = 0.006 for MAP2 Intensity, p = 0.015 for MAP2 dispersion value), suggesting senolytic D&Q administration is able to rescue neuronal dendritic damage after clearing senescent cells in the brain.

D&Q treatment reduced neuronal death and dendritic damage in mice hippocampus. A IF co-staining of NeuN and CL-Caspase 3 in hippocampal CA1 to assess neuronal death. B Quantitative analysis of Numbers of CL-Caspase 3-positive neurons and Relative Intensity of CL-Caspase 3 to Sham. C MAP2 staining was conducted to evaluate neuronal dendritic integrity. D Relative Intensity of MAP2 to Sham and MAP2 Dispersion values were quantified to examine dendritic structural integrity. Scale bar = 20 μm. N = 5. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI

Finally, behavioral tests were carried out to examine if D&Q treatment could positively change the functional outcome. Barnes Maze Task was adopted at 12 weeks after GCI to probe the hippocampus-dependent spatial reference memory. During the 3-day training stage, GCI mice exhibited longer escape latency to find the target hole as compared to Sham group ( p < 0.001 on Day 2, p < 0.001 on Day 3), which was reversed by D&Q treatment (Fig. 6 A, a, p = 0.009 on Day 2, p = 0.022 on Day 3). Identical escape velocities among these groups suggested the detected differences were not caused by velocity variation (Fig. 6 A, a). In the probe stage, GCI mice had decreased quadrant occupancy ( p < 0.001) and higher exploring errors ( p < 0.001) in the target zone compared with Sham, whereas mice following D&Q treatment exhibited higher quadrant occupancy and lower exploring errors (Fig. 6 A, b, p = 0.037 and 0.006, respectively). These data demonstrate D&Q treatment has pronounced effects in improving GCI-induced impairment in the spatial reference memory.

D&Q treatment attenuated the behavioral deficits after GCI. A Representative tracking plots of the 3rd day training in the Barnes Maze test, which is widely used to examine the hippocampus-dependent spatial reference memory ( a ). Escape latency and escape velocity during 3 consecutive days training were recorded ( a ). Representative tracking plots for the probe stage of Barnes Maze test were presented ( b ), the quadrant occupancy time as well as exploration errors were also analyzed ( b ). B Hippocampus-dependent recognition memory was evaluated by novel object recognition test. Tracking plots during the choice stage were displayed. Exploring time for familiar and novel objects were recorded, and the discrimination index were quantified. C Open field test was conducted to probe the anxiety level with exploring time in the central zone, and locomotor function with total travel distance. D Tail suspension test was carried out to examine the depression level by total immobility time. N = 8. # p < 0.05 vs. Sham, & p < 0.05 vs. GCI. $ p < 0.05 vs. Familiar object

To further assess the effects of GCI and D&Q on recognition memory, novel object recognition test was next performed at 13 weeks after GCI. As shown in Fig. 6 B, GCI mice displayed less time in exploring novel object as compared to Sham as evidenced by decreased discrimination index ( p = 0.002), indicative of impaired recognition memory. Interestingly, D&Q treatment can effectively rescue this deficit by elevating the exploring time on novel object (Fig. 6 B, p = 0.019). Open field test was further carried out at 13 weeks after GCI to evaluate the anxiety level and locomotor function after D&Q treatment (Fig. 6 C). Mice after GCI spent less time in the central zone of the open arena ( p = 0.01), suggest an elevated anxiety level compared with Sham. In contrast, GCI mice following D&Q administration spent significantly higher time in the central zone ( p = 0.042), indicative of improved anxiety. Interestingly, there were no differences in total travel distances, suggesting an unaltered locomotor function. Finally, we performed tail suspension test at 13 weeks after GCI to probe the depression levels. Our results suggested GCI mice had higher immobility time during the tail hanging ( p = 0.005), indicative of apparent depressive-like behavior (Fig. 6 D). Whereas D&Q treatment can effectively decrease the immobility time of GCI mice ( p = 0.041), suggesting attenuated depression level (Fig. 6 D).
sections.discussion:
While the beneficial effects of senolytics Dasatinib plus Quercetin have been widely reported, its roles in global cerebral ischemic brain injury are still unknown. In current study, we provided leading evidences and demonstrated that post-GCI D&Q treatment can significantly eliminate glial senescence and yield profound neuroprotective effects and functional preservation. The results from our study demonstrated D&Q treatment plays some key roles in ischemic injury to the brain, including: (1) suppressing the senescence and activation of hippocampal astrocyte and microglia; (2) reducing the production of senescence-associated secretory phenotypes; (3) inhibiting mitochondrial fragmentation and metabolic dysfunction; (4) reversing the decline of mitochondrial antioxidant ability and oxidative damage to protein structures; (5) enhancing neuronal structural integrity, attenuating neuronal death; (6) preserving hippocampus-dependent cognition, anxiety and depression-like behaviors.

Cellular senescence occurs in response to a variety of cellular stressors and leads to a state of irreversible growth arrest (Regulski 2017 ). Physiologically, cellular senescence plays an important role in neonatal development, wound healing and tissue remolding by activating and interacting with the immune cells. Senescent cells facilitate tissue remodeling and repair by secreting SASP that recruits immune cells and modifies the extracellular matrix (Liu et al. 2023 ). During neonatal development, senescent cells promote tissue remolding and morphogenesis by eliminating transient structures and modulating the abundance of different cell populations (Munoz-Espin and Serrano 2014 ). While cellular senescence is necessary for many physiological processes, senescent cells accumulate with aging and various neurological disorders, and impede the neural recovery. Studies in past decades have shown brain injury can accelerate brain aging, inflammaging and senescence (Amgalan et al. 2022 ; Hammond et al. 2019 ; Ritzel et al. 2023 ). Both observational and case–control studies revealed a “dose-dependent” effect of TBI on brain aging and later development of dementia. For instance, young adults with traumatic neurological deficits showed similar cognitive decline in elderly populations without traumatic neurological history (Faden and Loane 2015 ; Irimia et al. 2014 ). Whereas moderate-severe brain injury could potently facilitate the development of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Pupillo et al. 2020 ; Mackay et al. 2019 ; Fann et al. 2018 ; Gardner et al. 2015 ; Deutsch et al. 2015 ).

Emerging evidences also suggested that cellular senescence as a characteristic of neurological deficits, is closely associated with poor prognosis of ischemic stroke (Fu et al. 2023 ; Li et al. 2023 ). Acute stroke injury triggers high expression of both p16 and p21 mRNA restricted to the infarct area in the tMCAO brain, as well as surged pro-inflammatory SASP release (Torres-Querol et al. 2021 ). Interestingly, both p16 and p21 were mainly observed in cytoplasm/membrane of microglial cells and neurons, despite the controversy over whether p16/p21 should be considered as reliable senescence markers of post-mitotic neurons. A recent study from Fu et al. analyzed transcriptome data from multiple datasets and identified robust expression of senescence-related genes such as Angptl4 , Ccl3 , Ccl7 , Cxcl16 and Tnf in various brain regions after stroke (Fu et al. 2023 ). MG4 microglia which is highly correlated with cellular senescence in MCAO models, play a crucial role in stroke pathological progression. Study from Li et al. found robust senescence of blood–brain barrier (BBB) and following BBB breakdown in aged stroke mice, which can be rejuvenated by inducible pluripotent stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (Li et al. 2023 ). Similarly, senescent astrocytes induced after neuronal injury, play an integral role in the initiation and progression of following neurodegeneration and cognitive deficits (Cohen and Torres 2019 ). For instance, astrocyte senescence-like response was observed after chronic constrictive injury, followed by enhanced spinal proinflammatory factors (Du et al. 2023 ). Moreover, senescent astrocytes and microglia were detected in multiple brain regions after chronic brain injury, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, corpus callosum and lateral posterior thalamus (Wang et al. 2023 ). In our current study, we provided leading evidences that ischemic brain injury can trigger robust glial senescence in the hippocampus, which is characterized by strong p16 INK4a expression in both microglia and astrocytes.

Accumulating studies have demonstrated that clearance of senescent cells by either pharmaceutical or genetic approaches exhibit prominent benefits in improving disease progression and attenuating neurodegeneration. Genetic elimination of p16 INK4a positive senescent cells delayed the onset of aging-associated phenotypes and extended the healthy lifespan of progeroid mice (Farr et al. 2017 ; Baker et al. 2011 ). Similar studies showed that genetic clearance of AP1 activity in senescent glia alleviated the senescence markers, prevented lipid accumulation and extended life span in drosophila (Byrns et al. 2024 ). These exciting results strongly pushed the development of senotherapeutic agents which can effectively target and remove senescent cells. As senescent cells display resistance to cell death, senotherapeutics triggering the pro-apoptotic pathways in senescent cells have been identified as a promising strategy in aging and chronic neurological disorders. Currently known senolytic agents can be categorized into several classes based on their action mechanisms: kinase inhibitors, BCL-2 family inhibitors, p53 inhibitors, heat shock protein 90 inhibitors and histone deacetylase inhibitors. Among the reported senolytics, Dasatinib and Quercetin are two of the most studied senolytic drugs, and have exhibited prominent efficacy and less side effects in eliminating cellular senescence in both mice and human (Islam et al. 2023 ; Wissler Gerdes et al. 2020 ; Hickson et al. 2019 ; Xu et al. 2018 ).

Dasatinib is an FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor for the treatment of Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia via promotion of cellular death (Kirkland and Tchkonia 2020 ; Wissler Gerdes et al. 2020 ). While quercetin is a naturally occurring flavonoid compound that effectively removes senescent endothelial cells with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Xu et al. 2018 ; Zhu et al. 2015 ). Combined Dasatinib and Quercetin treatment as widely used senolytic therapy has shown potent anti-senescent and protective effects in age-related diseases. For instance, senolytic D&Q administration attenuated intestinal senescence and modulated the inflammatory environment of gut microbiome in aged mice (Saccon et al. 2021 ). Moreover, D&Q treatment improves cognitive abilities in aged Wistar rats via alleviating inflammation and modulating histone H3 methylation profile in the hippocampus (Krzystyniak et al. 2022 ). Recent study suggested long-term D&Q treatment after TBI can potently clear disease-associated glial senescence in multiple brain regions and improve the functional outcome (Wang et al. 2023 ). In this study, to our knowledge, we firstly reported that chronic D&Q treatment significantly decreased the senescence buildup of both microglia and astrocytes in mice hippocampus after GCI. By a series of behavioral tests, we further demonstrated that D&Q administration is effective to improve the GCI-induced cognitive decline, anxiety and depressive symptoms.

Cellular senescence drives several downstream pathological conditions, and one of the consequences is mitochondrial dysfunction. Impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular metabolism have been identified as hallmarks of cellular senescence, and dysfunctional mitochondria in return can drive the development of senescence phenotype and SASP secretion (Miwa et al. 2022 ; Martini and Passos 2023 ). Mitochondria are known as the powerhouse and metabolic signaling center of cells and are responsible for energy production by oxidative phosphorylation (Al Amir Dache and Thierry 2023 ; Monzel et al. 2023 ; Annesley and Fisher 2019 ). In addition, mitochondria mediate intercellular communication, govern the protein quality control, translocation and metabolite transport (Pfanner et al. 2019 ). Considering its essential roles in regulating cellular functions, mitochondrial deficit is considered as a key mechanism underlying aging, cancer and neurodegenerative diseases (Annesley and Fisher 2019 ). Numerous studies suggested that senescent cells have declined mitochondrial respiratory capacity and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) (Rizza et al. 2018 ; Correia-Melo et al. 2016 ; Passos et al. 2007 ). Low mitochondrial MMP is associated with elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS), which further contributes to increased cellular oxidative damage (Sun et al. 2016 ; Passos et al. 2010 ). In return, unbalanced ROS production due to mitochondrial dysfunction induces senescence by transforming protein conformation, changing protein–protein and protein-DNA interactions (Erusalimsky 2020 ).

Another hallmark of impaired mitochondria in cellular senescence is significant change in mitochondrial organization, which is typically characterized by unbalanced fission and fusion dynamics (Jendrach et al. 2005 ). It was indicated that mitochondria exhibited elongated, hyperfused morphology during senescence, which may imply acute energetic need after metabolic deficiency (Cogliati et al. 2016 ). However, in present study our results suggested that in chronic GCI stage, senescent mitochondria underwent significantly increased fragmentation as well as reduced CCO activity and ATP production, indicating upregulated fission over fusion processes and subsequent metabolic failure. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction leads to declined activities of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes, such as Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), superoxide dismutase, mitochondrial glutathione (mGSH) and catalase, etc. (Napolitano et al. 2021 ). Consistently, we found reduced expression of SOD2, a key enzyme that manages ROS clearance in mitochondria, along with increased protein oxidation after GCI. Whereas long-term senolytic D&Q treatment curbed these mitochondrial deficits and enhanced the neuronal survival and functional outcome in ischemic mice. These findings demonstrated maintaining mitochondrial integrity and rescuing the metabolic and antioxidant functions could be an essential mechanism underlying the beneficial effects of senolytic D&Q therapy. However, one remaining question is whether Dasatinib or Quercetin is primarily responsible for promoting mitochondrial integrity after GCI is still unclear, further study is needed to address this issue.
sections.conclusion: Our study demonstrated that D&Q treatment has profound neuroprotective effects by lowering the expression of glial senescence in the brain and suppressing the SASP release. Although the beneficial effects of D&Q treatment could be attributed to complex mechanisms, our results suggested that maintaining mitochondrial integrity, improving the metabolic functions and enhancing mitochondrial antioxidant ability could be the essential downstream pathways through which senolytic D&Q exerts neuroprotection. In summary, these findings shed light on a pronounced beneficial role of combined D&Q treatment in global cerebral ischemic brain injury. Our study provided novel insights for future clinical application of senolytic agents in GCI encephalopathy therapy.
